explanation: James Watt coined 'horsepower' to sell his engines by comparing them with draught horses. One mechanical horsepower is about 746 watts.

claims.text: The watt, the SI unit of power, is named after James Watt, the Scottish engineer known for improving the steam engine.

The joule (energy) is named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule, the newton (force) after the English scientist Isaac Newton, and the volt (electric potential) after the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta; none is a unit of power.
James Watt coined the term horsepower, comparing the output of his steam engines with that of draught horses to market them.
One mechanical horsepower is about 746 watts.

evidence.restatement: The SI derived unit of power, one joule per second, honours James Watt (1736 to 1819), the Scot whose separate condenser made steam engines far more efficient.

claimResults.note: Unit named for Watt (adopted by the British Association in 1882, SI later). Watt was born in Greenock, Scotland, and 'improving' (not inventing) the steam engine is the accurate description. Key unique among the options.

evidence.restatement: The energy unit honours the English physicist J. P. Joule, the force unit the English scientist Isaac Newton, and the potential-difference unit the Italian Alessandro Volta; power is none of their quantities.

claimResults.note: All three distractors are SI units named after people, same kind as the key, but none is a unit of power and none of their namesakes was a Scottish steam engineer, so each is definitely wrong.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Thomas Savery introduced the underlying comparison, and James Watt turned it into the named unit. ... Savery's 1702 book The Miner's Friend compared an engine's output to the number of horses needed to do the same work. ... Sources disagree on when the term appeared.

evidence.restatement: Watt defined horsepower as a unit (about 33,000 foot-pounds per minute) in the early 1780s to rate his engines against the horses they replaced, but comparisons of engines with horses, by Savery in 1702, came earlier.

claimResults.note: I am certain Watt defined and popularized horsepower as a unit for marketing his engines, but not certain he coined the word: references I know say he 'adopted' the term, and Savery's 1702 Miner's Friend already rated engines by horses. My one search returned only Tier C pages, which split between 'coined' and 'adopted' and give conflicting dates. So 'coined' is not confirmed. Suggested fix: 'James Watt defined horsepower as a unit to sell his engines, comparing them with draught horses.'

evidence.restatement: Mechanical (imperial) horsepower is defined as 550 foot-pounds-force per second, which works out to 745.7 W.

claimResults.note: 550 ft·lbf/s x 0.3048 m/ft x 4.448222 N/lbf = 745.70 W, so 'about 746 watts' is right; the claim correctly specifies mechanical horsepower (metric horsepower is about 735.5 W).

issues.note: c3 uncertain: the explanation says Watt 'coined' horsepower. Watt certainly defined the unit and used it to market his engines, but the word or horse comparison has earlier use (Savery, 1702), and the search found only Tier C pages that conflict. Reword to 'defined' or 'popularized'; the key and distractors are unaffected.

evidence.restatement: The SI unit of power, the watt, honours the Scottish engineer James Watt, whose changes made the steam engine far more efficient.

claimResults.note: Rival test: horsepower is also a power unit named for no person and is not offered; joule, volt and newton measure energy, potential and force. Only one option is a unit of power, and it is named for Watt.

evidence.restatement: Joule, newton and volt honour James Prescott Joule (English), Isaac Newton (English) and Alessandro Volta (Italian) and measure energy, force and electric potential.

claimResults.note: Nationality labels are right. Newton is often called 'English physicist and mathematician'; 'scientist' is fine.

evidence.restatement: Watt devised the horsepower measure in the late 1700s to show customers how many draught horses an engine replaced.

claimResults.note: The account is the standard one; 'coined' is the usual wording.

evidence.restatement: A mechanical horsepower equals 745.7 watts, so about 746 W.

claimResults.note: The metric horsepower is 735.5 W, but the claim says mechanical, and 745.7 is right. High-risk number, so it leans on check A's external source.
